intro: Families keep many special days. Some light candles. Some share a big meal. Some keep no religious days at all. Every family's days matter to them.

In this unit, you will learn about special days like Christmas, Hanukkah, Eid, Diwali, Lunar New Year and Vaisakhi. You will visit places where people gather, like a church, a synagogue, a mosque, a temple and a gurdwara.
You will learn fair words, like "some families" and "Muslims celebrate." You will learn to ask a friend kind questions and to be a good guest.
bigQuestion: How do families keep special days and places, and how can we learn about them kindly?

timeline.t: Make a class calendar of special days
Learn about Diwali, the festival of lights
Learn about Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr
Learn about Lunar New Year and Vaisakhi
Visit a church, synagogue and mosque in words
Visit a temple and a gurdwara, and practice being a good guest

words.d: a special day that a family or group keeps each year
what a group of people believe and do together
to do happy, special things to mark a day
a candle holder lit for the eight nights of Hanukkah
a month when many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset
to pray, sing or show love to God or to what is holy
a free meal at a gurdwara, shared with anyone
a visitor to someone's home or place

test.q: Which holiday do many Christians keep on December 25?
test.why: Many Christians keep Christmas on December 25.

test.q: What do Jewish families light at Hanukkah?
When do Muslims celebrate Eid al-Fitr?
test.why: Eid al-Fitr comes at the end of Ramadan.

test.q: Diwali is a festival of what?
test.why: Diwali is a festival of lights.

test.q: Vaisakhi is special for which group?

test.why: Jewish people worship in a synagogue.

test.q: At a gurdwara, what does everyone do?
test.why: Everyone covers their head at a gurdwara.

test.q: Which way do Muslims face to pray?
A friend keeps no holiday. What is kind?
test.why: Some families keep no holiday, and that is okay.

write.prompt: Pick two special days or two places from this unit. Draw them. Then say one thing that is the same and one thing that is different. Use "some families" or name who keeps it.
tips: Say who keeps it, like "Sikhs" or "Christians."
Tell one thing the same and one thing different.

title: Families and Their Special Days

chapters.title: Special Days at Home
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do families keep special days, and how can we ask a friend about theirs?

story.title: A Light for Every Month
story.kicker: Mia's class makes a big calendar and finds something surprising.
paragraphs: Mia's class makes a big calendar. It hangs on the wall. Each child adds a special day from home. They draw it in the right month.
Sam draws candles in December. His family keeps Hanukkah. Priya draws small clay lamps in the fall. Her family keeps Diwali. Omar draws a moon for Eid.

Mia draws a tree with lights for Christmas. Leo draws red lanterns for Lunar New Year. Jas draws a parade in April for Vaisakhi. Ben says his family has no holiday. They have a big pancake day on his birthday.
The class steps back. There are lights in many months! Their teacher smiles. "Every family has its own days," she says. "Each one matters to that family."
story.think: What is one day that is special in your home? What do you do that day?

lessons.title: Days That Matter
lessons.mainIdea: Families keep different special days, and each day matters to them.
reading: A holiday is a special day. Families do special things on it. They eat, sing and spend time together.
Different families keep different days. Some days come from a religion. A religion is what a group of people believe and do together.
Some families keep no religious days. They may have other special days, like birthdays. Every family's days are real to them.

words.d: a special day that a family or group keeps each year
what a group of people believe and do together, like prayer and holidays

look.title: A Picture in Words
look.text: Look at the big calendar on the wall. There are candles in December. There is a moon in spring. There is a lantern in winter. Each picture is a day that one family keeps.
look.prompt: Pick one picture. What might that family do on their day?

check.q: What is a holiday?
choices: A special day a family or group keeps each year
A day with no school work at all
check.why: A holiday is a special day kept each year.

check.q: Do all families keep the same special days?
choices: Yes, every family keeps the same days
check.why: Different families keep different days.

check.q: Ben's family keeps no religious holiday. What is true?
choices: His family's special days still matter
His family is doing something wrong
check.why: Some families keep no religious days. Their days are real to them.

lessons.title: Saying "Some Families"
lessons.mainIdea: We say "some families" or "Muslims celebrate" to speak fairly about each day.
reading: Words can be kind and true. We say "some families keep Diwali." We do not say "everyone keeps Diwali."
We name who keeps a day. "Muslims celebrate Eid." "Christians celebrate Christmas." "Jewish families light Hanukkah candles." This tells who, and it is fair to all.

words.d: to do happy, special things to mark a day

look.title: Two Ways to Say It
look.text: Kai says, "Everybody has a Christmas tree." Nia says, "Many Christian families put up a Christmas tree."
look.prompt: Which way fits more families? Why?

check.q: Which words are fair to all families?
check.why: "Some families" is true. Not every family keeps the same day.

check.q: Who celebrates Eid?
check.why: Muslims celebrate Eid.

check.q: What does celebrate mean?
choices: To do happy, special things to mark a day
check.why: Celebrate means to mark a day with happy, special things.

lessons.title: Christmas and Hanukkah
lessons.mainIdea: Christians keep Christmas and Jewish families keep Hanukkah, often in December.
reading: Christmas is on December 25 for many Christians. Christians believe Jesus was born on this day long ago. Many families give gifts and sing. Some put up a tree with lights.
Hanukkah is a Jewish holiday. It lasts eight nights. Families light a menorah. They add one more candle each night. Many eat potato pancakes called latkes.

words.d: a candle holder; at Hanukkah it holds candles for eight nights, plus one helper candle
the day many Christians remember the birth of Jesus

look.title: A Line Read at Christmas
look.text: For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.
look.cite: The Bible, Luke 2:11, King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Christians read these words at Christmas. Whose birth do they tell about?

check.q: How many nights does Hanukkah last?
check.why: Hanukkah lasts eight nights.

check.q: Which holiday do many Christians keep on December 25?
check.why: Many Christians keep Christmas on December 25.

check.q: What do Jewish families light at Hanukkah?
choices: A lantern for the new year
check.why: At Hanukkah, Jewish families light a menorah.

lessons.title: Diwali, Festival of Lights
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus, Sikhs and Jains keep Diwali with small lamps and bright colors.
reading: Diwali is a festival of lights. It comes in the fall. Many Hindus keep it. Many Sikhs and Jains mark it too.
Families light small clay lamps called diyas. They make bright patterns on the floor. They share sweets. Many Hindus say the lights show good winning over bad.

words.d: a fall festival of lights kept by many Hindus, Sikhs and Jains
a small clay lamp lit at Diwali

look.title: Lamps by the Door
look.text: Look at the front step. A row of tiny clay lamps glows. Each has a small flame. On the floor is a flower pattern in pink, yellow and blue powder.
look.prompt: Which holiday is this? What clues tell you?

check.q: What is a diya?
check.why: A diya is a small clay lamp lit at Diwali.

check.q: When does Diwali usually come?
check.why: Diwali comes in the fall.

check.q: Who keeps Diwali?
check.why: Many Hindus keep Diwali. Many Sikhs and Jains mark it too.

lessons.title: Eid al-Fitr
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims celebrate Eid al-Fitr at the end of Ramadan, a month of fasting.
reading: Ramadan is a special month for Muslims. Many grown-ups fast. They do not eat or drink from dawn to sunset. Each evening, families share a meal.
When Ramadan ends, Muslims celebrate Eid al-Fitr. Families pray together. They wear new or nice clothes. They visit, share food and give to people in need.

words.d: a month when many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset
to not eat or drink for a time

look.title: The Month of Ramadan
look.text: The Qur'an says that fasting is asked of believers in the month of Ramadan. It says God wants ease for people, not hardship.
look.cite: The Qur'an, Surah 2 (Al-Baqarah), verses 183-185, retold in plain words
look.prompt: What does this passage say Muslims do in Ramadan?

check.q: What do Muslims celebrate when Ramadan ends?
check.why: Eid al-Fitr comes at the end of Ramadan.

check.q: What does fast mean?
choices: To not eat or drink for a time
check.why: To fast means to not eat or drink for a time.

check.q: In Ramadan, when do many Muslims share a meal?
check.why: Many Muslims fast until sunset, then share a meal.

lessons.title: Lunar New Year and Vaisakhi
lessons.mainIdea: Many families mark a new year in winter or spring, like Lunar New Year and Vaisakhi.
reading: Lunar New Year starts with a new moon in winter. Many Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese families keep it. They clean the house. They eat a big meal. Children may get red envelopes with money.
Vaisakhi comes in April. It is a special day for Sikhs. Sikhs visit the gurdwara, their place of worship. Many join a parade with music and prayer songs.

words.d: a new year that starts with a new moon in winter
a spring day in April that is special for Sikhs

look.title: Special Days on Our Calendar
look.cite: Common calendar facts; some dates move each year
look.prompt: Which day comes first in the year? Which comes last?

check.q: What might a child get at Lunar New Year?
check.why: Many children get red envelopes at Lunar New Year.

check.q: Vaisakhi is a special day for which group?
check.why: Vaisakhi is special for Sikhs.

check.q: Lunar New Year starts with what?
check.why: Lunar New Year starts with a new moon.

lessons.title: Good Questions
lessons.mainIdea: We can ask a friend kindly about their special day and listen well.
reading: Your friend's day may be new to you. You can ask about it! Ask kind questions. "What do you do on your special day?"
Listen to the answer. Do not say a day is weird. Say "thank you for telling me." Your friend may not keep any holiday. That is okay too.

words.d: to treat people and what matters to them with care

look.title: At the Lunch Table
look.text: Omar says, "Tomorrow is Eid!" Lily does not know Eid. She could say, "That's weird." Or she could say, "Cool! What do you do on Eid?"
look.prompt: What should Lily say? Why is that kind?

check.q: Which question is kind?
choices: "What do you do on your special day?"
check.why: A kind question asks and listens.

check.q: What does respect mean?
choices: To treat people and what matters to them with care
check.why: Respect means treating people with care.

check.q: Your friend keeps no holiday. What do you do?
choices: Tell them they must pick one
check.why: Some families keep no holiday. That is okay.

lessons.title: Being Together
lessons.mainIdea: Most special days share lights, food, songs and being together.
reading: The days are different. But many share things. Many have lights. Many have good food. Many have songs or prayers.
Most of all, many special days bring people together. Families, friends and neighbors meet. They share and help each other.

words.d: something a family or group does the same way year after year

look.title: Same and Different
look.text: Hanukkah has candles. Diwali has clay lamps. Christmas has lights on a tree. Eid has a big family meal. Lunar New Year has a big family meal too.
look.prompt: What is the same about these days? What is different?

check.q: What do Hanukkah and Diwali both have?
check.why: Both use lights: candles and clay lamps.

check.q: What is a tradition?
choices: Something done the same way year after year
check.why: A tradition is done the same way year after year.

check.q: Eid and Lunar New Year both have what?
check.why: Both have a big family meal.

review.q: Which holiday has eight nights of candles?
review.why: Jewish families light candles for eight nights of Hanukkah.

review.q: Muslims celebrate Eid al-Fitr after which month?
review.why: Eid al-Fitr comes when Ramadan ends.

review.q: Which holiday has clay lamps called diyas?
Vaisakhi is a special day for whom?

review.why: We name who keeps a day. Muslims celebrate Eid.

review.q: A family keeps no religious holiday. What is true?
review.why: Every family's days are real to them.

chapters.title: Places Where People Gather
chapters.bigQuestion: What do people do in places of worship, and how can we be a good guest?

story.title: Five Doors on One Street
story.kicker: Theo walks down one Chicago street and sees five special doors.
paragraphs: Theo walks with his grandpa down a long Chicago street. "Look," says Grandpa. "Five doors. Each opens on a special day."
On Friday, people go into a mosque. Some take off their shoes. Friday evening, families walk to a synagogue. On Saturday, they read from a big scroll.
On Sunday, bells ring at a church. People sing inside. Down the block is a Hindu temple with bright colors. Next is a gurdwara. People cover their heads and share a free meal.
"Do we go in one?" Theo asks. "Not every family does," says Grandpa. "Some do, and some do not. But we can learn about all of them."
story.think: What did Theo see at each door? Which place would you like to learn about?

lessons.title: A Place to Gather
lessons.mainIdea: A place of worship is where a group meets to pray, sing, read and learn.
reading: Worship means to pray, sing or show love to God or to what is holy. Many religions have a special building for it.
People gather there. They pray. They sing. They read from holy books. They learn and eat together. Not every family goes to one. That is okay.

words.d: to pray, sing or show love to God or to what is holy
very special and set apart, for people of a religion

look.title: What Do You Hear?
look.text: Close your eyes. You hear people singing together. Someone reads out loud. Then it is quiet while people pray. After, you smell food and hear friends talk.
look.prompt: What are the people doing in this place?

check.q: What is a place of worship?
choices: A place where a group meets to pray and learn
check.why: People gather there to pray, sing and learn.

check.q: Does every family go to a place of worship?
check.why: Not every family goes. That is okay.

check.q: What does worship mean?
choices: To pray, sing or show love to God or what is holy
check.why: Worship means to pray, sing or show love to God or what is holy.

lessons.title: Holy Days to Gather
lessons.mainIdea: Many groups gather on a special day each week.
reading: Many Muslims gather at a mosque at midday on Friday. They pray together. Then they may visit with friends.
The Jewish Sabbath, Shabbat, starts Friday at sunset. It ends Saturday night. Many Jewish families go to a synagogue. Many Christians go to church on Sunday.

words.d: a day of rest; for Jewish families, from Friday sunset to Saturday night

look.title: Weekly Gathering Days
rows: Jewish families at a synagogue: Saturday
look.cite: Common weekly practice; some groups gather on other days too
look.prompt: Which group gathers last in the week?

check.q: When do many Muslims gather to pray together?
check.why: Many Muslims pray together at a mosque on Friday.

check.q: When does Shabbat start?
check.why: Shabbat starts Friday at sunset.

check.q: Many Christians go to church on which day?
check.why: Many Christians go to church on Sunday.

lessons.title: Church and Synagogue
lessons.mainIdea: Christians gather in churches; Jewish people gather in synagogues.
reading: A church is where Christians worship. Many have a cross. Some have tall towers and bells. Inside, people sing, pray and read from the Bible.
A synagogue is where Jewish people worship. Inside is a cabinet called the ark. It holds the Torah scroll. The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible.

words.d: a building where Christians worship
a building where Jewish people worship and learn
the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, written on a scroll

look.title: Glad to Go
look.text: I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.
look.cite: The Bible, Psalm 122:1, King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: This song is in both the Jewish and Christian Bible. How does the singer feel about going?

check.q: What is kept in the ark in a synagogue?
check.why: The ark holds the Torah scroll.

check.q: Where do Christians worship?
check.why: Christians worship in a church.

check.q: What is the Torah?
choices: The first five books of the Hebrew Bible
check.why: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible.

lessons.title: The Mosque
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims pray in a mosque, often on soft rugs, facing toward Mecca.
reading: A mosque is where Muslims pray. Many have a round dome. Some have a tall tower called a minaret.
People take off their shoes. They wash before they pray. They stand in rows on soft rugs. They all face toward Mecca, a holy city in Saudi Arabia.

words.d: a building where Muslims pray
a holy city for Muslims; they face toward it to pray

look.title: Rows on the Rug
look.text: Look inside. There are no chairs. A big soft rug covers the floor. People stand in straight rows, side by side. Shoes wait in a rack by the door.
look.prompt: Why do you think the shoes are by the door?

check.q: What do people do with their shoes in a mosque?
check.why: People take off their shoes in a mosque.

check.q: Which way do Muslims face to pray?
check.why: Muslims face toward Mecca to pray.

check.q: What is a minaret?
choices: A tall tower on some mosques
check.why: A minaret is a tall tower on some mosques.

lessons.title: A Hindu Temple
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus visit a temple to pray and see images of the gods.
reading: A Hindu temple is often bright and full of carvings. People take off their shoes. Some ring a bell as they come in.
Inside are images of gods and goddesses. Hindus bring gifts like flowers, fruit and light. They pray and sing. Many Hindus pray at home too.

words.d: a building where some groups, like Hindus, worship

look.title: Gifts at the Temple
look.text: A girl holds a plate. On it are orange flowers, a banana and a tiny flame. She rings a bell. Then she steps up to pray.
look.prompt: What gifts does she bring? What might they show?

check.q: What might Hindus bring to a temple?
check.why: Hindus bring gifts like flowers and fruit.

check.q: Where do Hindus worship?
choices: At a temple and at home
check.why: Hindus pray at temples and at home.

check.q: What might someone ring when they come into a Hindu temple?
check.why: Some ring a bell as they come in.

lessons.title: The Gurdwara
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhs gather at a gurdwara, where anyone can share a free meal.
reading: A gurdwara is where Sikhs worship. Their holy book is the Guru Granth Sahib. People sing its hymns.
Everyone covers their head and takes off their shoes. After prayer comes langar. Langar is a free meal. Everyone sits together and eats. Anyone may come, of any faith.

words.d: a building where Sikhs worship
a free meal at a gurdwara, shared with anyone who comes

look.title: Everyone at One Meal
look.text: Look at the long hall. People sit side by side on the floor. Helpers bring bowls of lentils and warm bread. No one pays. A grandma, a student and a visitor eat together.
look.prompt: What does this meal show about Sikh ideas of sharing?

check.q: What is langar?
choices: A free meal shared with anyone
check.why: Langar is a free meal at a gurdwara.

check.q: What is the Sikh holy book?
check.why: Sikhs read the Guru Granth Sahib.

check.q: Who can eat langar?
check.why: Anyone may come to langar.

lessons.title: Guest Manners
lessons.mainIdea: A good guest uses a quiet voice and follows the rules of the place.
reading: You might visit a place of worship with a friend. Be a good guest! Use a quiet voice. Watch what others do.
Some places ask you to take off your shoes. Some ask you to cover your head. If you are not sure, ask kindly. You can watch without joining in.

words.d: a visitor to someone's home or place

look.title: Visiting with a Friend
look.text: Ava visits a gurdwara with her friend Harpreet. She sees a basket of head scarves by the door. People are taking off their shoes. It is quiet inside.
look.prompt: What should Ava do? How can she find out?

check.q: What voice should a guest use?
check.why: A good guest uses a quiet voice.

check.q: You are not sure what to do. What helps?
check.why: Asking kindly helps.

check.q: At a gurdwara, what do guests do?
check.why: Everyone covers their head at a gurdwara.

lessons.title: A Walk in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago has many kinds of places of worship, close together.
reading: Chicago has people from all over the world. So it has many places of worship. You can find churches, synagogues, mosques, temples and gurdwaras.
Near Chicago, in Wilmette, is the Baha'i House of Worship. It is white and has nine sides. People of all faiths may visit it.

words.d: a person who lives near you

look.title: Our Street Walk
look.text: Pretend to walk one block. First, a church with a bell. Next, a synagogue with a star on the door. Then a mosque with a dome. Last, a gurdwara with a tall flag.
look.prompt: Which place did you pass first? Which one would you ask about?

check.q: Why does Chicago have many places of worship?
choices: People came from all over the world
It is a very small town
check.why: People from all over the world live in Chicago.

check.q: What is in Wilmette, near Chicago?
check.why: The Baha'i House of Worship is in Wilmette.

check.q: How many sides does the Baha'i House of Worship have?
check.why: It has nine sides.

review.q: What holy book is kept in a synagogue's ark?
review.why: The ark holds the Torah scroll.

choices: A free meal at a gurdwara
review.why: Langar is a free meal at a gurdwara.

review.q: What should a good guest do if not sure?
Many Christians go to church on which day?
review.why: Many Christians go to church on Sunday.

review.q: Where might you take off your shoes?
choices: In a mosque or a Hindu temple
review.why: Shoes come off in a mosque, a Hindu temple and a gurdwara.
